nodes.desc: Refuses to run with assertions compiled out. Several security controls in this tree are spelled as asserts (the path-traversal check in custody.tokens.token_path, the "d" not in jwk check that stands between a library change and the co-signer publishing its signing key, the empty-binding check in quote_policy._binds, the length and version checks in cosigner.keys.unwrap), and under -O every one of them disappears while the process keeps running. Called at import by backend/__init__.py and, separately, by cosigner/__init__.py, which imports nothing from backend and so cannot rely on its guard.

The attest-before-run gate, executed by the container entrypoint before the daemon or the webhook start. Under TEE_REQUIRED it exits 1 rather than starting anything unless the CVM genuinely attests, the KMS released the secrets, the running measurement matches the expected one, and none of secrets.volume_secrets() is present on disk. The fail-closed rule is about one value above all: if we cannot prove we run attested, we must not touch a mailbox. Outside a CVM (laptop, plain Hetzner box) it degrades to a warning so a checkout still runs.

The only code that speaks to the dstack guest agent, over the unix socket /var/run/dstack.sock mounted into the container by docker-compose. GET /Info returns app_id, instance_id, compose_hash and the measurements; POST /GetKey is the KMS unseal primitive, released only to an attested CVM; POST /GetQuote binds up to 64 bytes of report_data into a TDX quote; POST /GetTlsKey mints the RA-TLS keypair whose certificate carries the quote.

The five checks that decide whether a TDX quote is one we authorized, in the order a failure should be reported: parse and is-TDX, report_data binding, measurements against an allowlist, signature chain to the Intel root through PCCS collateral, then TCB status and advisories. Two callers verify quotes in opposite directions and must not drift, so the parsing, the allowlist rules, the TCB policy and the caching live here and each caller supplies only what is its own: where the quote came from, and what report_data must bind. Policy.match() takes a scope so one allowlist file can serve several verified things without one entry silently authorizing another, and mr_td may never be null.

quote_policy is exported via the ✳ proxy convention: its two consumers sit at opposite ends of the diagram (the co-signer checking an inbound RA-TLS certificate, inference attestation checking an outbound provider), so each is drawn with a small 'quote_policy ✳' chip beside it rather than two full-height lines.

Single source of truth for how a secret reaches this process. The only read of .env (idempotent, and injected environment always wins over the file), the only definition of "this value is present" (answered by calling the same code the services call: PolarBilling(), telegram.operator_target(), oauth_app.load_keys()), and the only place a secret is named in a log without being printed (fingerprint()). Under TEE_REQUIRED no file is read at all and volume_secrets() names exactly the files whose mere presence fails the boot gate.

secrets.load() is exported via the ✳ proxy convention: nearly every band consumes a secret, so each consumer is drawn with a small 'secrets.load() ✳' chip beside it rather than a bundle of full-height lines from this node.

The Google OAuth application itself: client_id, client_secret, scopes, endpoints. One app serves every user, so the widest-blast-radius value the deployment holds is read in exactly one place. load_keys() takes the injected GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID / GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET pair first and refuses the .gmail-mcp/ volume file entirely under TEE_REQUIRED, because that file is one the KMS does not gate and the measurement does not cover.

The confidential-VM side of the platform. Releases the app_secret only to a CVM whose measurement the KMS has authorized, and signs TDX quotes over report_data the enclave supplies. Reached only through dstack_client over the mounted unix socket.

Provisioning certificate cache service. Supplies the collateral (TCB info, QE identity, CRLs) that lets a quote's signature chain be checked back to the Intel root, and that dates the TCB status. fetch_collateral() wraps dcap_qvl.get_collateral because it is a pyo3 builtin that grabs the running loop when called, so a naive asyncio.run() raises "no running event loop" and reads as a refused attestation rather than a broken one.
Signs in with Google, subscribes, generates a voice profile, writes their personal facts, links Telegram, picks an inference provider. Everything else the product does happens without them present.

The product web UI, a stdlib HTTP server behind Caddy on 127.0.0.1:8790. Public pages (home, about, FAQ, pricing, contact) plus the signed-in surface: dashboard, /voice (generates a profile from the account's own sent mail on a background thread and shows it as editable plaintext), /personal (the owner's own facts, kept in a second box precisely because generating a profile overwrites the profile), settings, billing. The standalone /onboard flow it superseded was removed; its OAuth sequence now lives in backend/onboarding/provisioning.py.

Public hostnames (APP_HOST, the product; API_HOST, the Pub/Sub push and Polar webhook box), loopback ports, and every externally visible URL built from them: the OAuth callback, the Polar webhook, the Pub/Sub audience. A hostname edited in two of the three places that must agree (the app, the Caddy site block, the third party's registration) is an outage, so deploy/render_caddyfile.py renders the proxy config from this module. COSIGNER_PORT is re-exported rather than defined, because it belongs beside the server that binds it.

HMAC-SHA256 signed session cookie of the form {email}:{iat}:{signature}. The cookie carries only the account email; everything else is looked up through account.py on each request. The secret's variable name is owned by backend/secrets.py rather than here, so nothing in backend/ reaches up into frontend/ to ask whether a session is configured.
Proxy for secrets.load() (see the ✳ node): supplies SESSION_SECRET, the key the session cookie is signed with.

The Google consent sequence, in one copy: auth URL with PKCE and dpop_jkt, code exchange, tokens.take_custody, register_account, watch registration, checkout redirect. handle_callback() is the whole decision path, HTTP-free and directly tested. The exchange is Python rather than a shelled-out Node call because Google binds a refresh token to a DPoP key at that one request and nowhere else, so the exchange has to sit next to backend.custody. Nothing about the token touches disk on the way through.

The per-account context threaded through every processing path: masking identity, state cursor, notification target, plan status, settings, and the custody record its Gmail access is derived from. A shared process holds one Account per user with no ambient single-tenant globals. load_accounts() drops inactive accounts, which is what makes a lapsed subscription unroutable end to end. The manifest is required: the box owner is a normal entry in it, seeded once, not an implicit fallback.

The multi-tenant account store: per-user identity, token file, telegram target, timezone, plan status, voice pointer, settings. Holds PII, so it is git-ignored and written 0600 inside a 0700 directory. Seeded once with `python -m backend.accounts.seed_owner`; every later entry arrives through register_account at the end of a successful consent.

Turns a Polar subscription into a local plan_status. Entitlement is one decision (subscription_entitled), used by both the instant webhook path and the periodic poller, so the two cannot disagree about what counts as paid. PLAN_PRICE_EUR is also the one place the quoted price lives: the landing copy, pricing page, comparison table, sign-up button and billing table each held their own literal and drifted from the Polar product, quoting €20 for a €25 subscription.
Proxy for secrets.load() (see the ✳ node): supplies the Polar organization token, product id and webhook secret.

Thin stdlib client for the two reads billing needs (resolve a customer's email, list subscriptions) plus the one write (mint a customer session so a signed-in user reaches the Polar-hosted portal without a second login).

Verifies the Standard Webhooks signature on a Polar order.paid / subscription.* event and routes it through PolarBilling.apply_event, flipping the buyer's plan_status the moment they pay. Runs as a loopback HTTP server behind Caddy on API_HOST. Polar quirk: the dashboard's webhook secret must be base64-encoded before it reaches the verifier, because Polar stores it raw and the library expects base64.
The periodic safety net behind the webhook: reconciles every local account's plan_status against Polar, catching missed webhook deliveries and lapsed subscriptions. Run by billing-poller.timer.

Where the user grants Gmail and Calendar scopes. The authorization request carries a PKCE challenge and dpop_jkt, the thumbprint of the co-signer's public key, which is what binds the resulting refresh token to a key this box does not hold.
The merchant of record. Polar is what actually charges, so changing the product there means changing PLAN_PRICE_EUR too.

The only path from a stored record to a usable access token, and the replacement for what google-auth used to do internally with a plaintext refresh token on disk. Every refresh is: read the outer ciphertext, ask the co-signer to unwrap-and-sign, open the inner layer, POST the refresh_token grant with the returned DPoP proof, zeroize, cache only the access token. Google answers the first proof with use_dpop_nonce, so the nonce round trip is mandatory rather than an optimization. Nothing on this box can produce an access token by itself.

The enclave's half of split custody: the inner encryption layer, keyed by HKDF from the dstack KMS app_secret, which is released only to a CVM whose measurement the KMS authorized. seal_inner/open_inner are the only functions that touch a plaintext refresh token and neither talks to the network. Outside a CVM a dev key from the environment stands in, but only while TEE_REQUIRED is unset: on a box that claims to be an enclave, a derived-from-nothing key would mean the tokens were never protected at all.

nodes.lbl:
layer order is the guarantee:
ours inside, theirs outside
nodes.desc: Reversed, the co-signer's unwrap would yield a plaintext refresh token and it would become the single box that can read every mailbox, which is the arrangement this design exists to avoid. Anything that changes the order silently destroys the property.

One user's refresh token under both layers: the co-signer's wrap on the outside, ours on the inside. Written 0600 inside a 0700 directory, and useless to anyone who reads it without the co-signer. The record carries a key version so a rotation is a readable migration rather than a guess.

The enclave's only channel to the co-signer, and the sole network boundary of split custody. Everything crossing this wire is either ciphertext the co-signer cannot open (inner), ciphertext it can only re-wrap (outer), or a signature over an HTTP request description. Unwrap and sign are one call rather than two: it halves the round trips and makes the co-signer's rate limit count refreshes rather than half-refreshes. There is deliberately no bypass: a co-signer that is unreachable means no mail is processed for anyone.

The refresh_token grant. Accepts the proof the co-signer signed and returns an access token that is plain Bearer, not DPoP-bound, which is why access tokens are cached for their hour and refresh tokens are not cached at all.

The co-signer's HTTP surface: POST /wrap, POST /unwrap-and-sign, POST /sign-dpop, GET /dpop-jwk, GET /health. Behind the one Caddy site block that demands a client certificate. /sign-dpop exists because the unwrap+sign pairing cannot cover every proof: at the authorization-code exchange there is no uid yet, since which mailbox consented is not known until the response comes back.

Paths, field names, the loopback port and the base64 codec, read by both halves. Two copies is what produced the first integration failure: both sides agreed on every path and field name and still could not talk, because one spelled binary as padded standard base64 and the other as unpadded base64url. A wrong codec surfaces as an AES-GCM tag failure, which this design reports as tampering, so the bug arrives disguised as an attack.

Is the thing on the other end of this connection the enclave we authorized? RA-TLS puts the TDX quote inside the enclave's own certificate, so the check costs no extra round trip. The cadence is per TLS connection, not per request: a quote is a boot-time measurement, the enclave mints a fresh RA-TLS keypair at each boot, and a boot is exactly when the measurement can change, so an unseen certificate fingerprint is the correct trigger for the full check.

The co-signer's own measurement allowlist, which is the point of the second machine: the enclave cannot edit it. A new compose_hash must be authorized here and in the AppAuth contract before deploying, or every unwrap fails.
Proxy for backend/tee/quote_policy.py (see the ✳ node): the same five checks, pointed inward at the client certificate that just arrived.

What the co-signer will do, how often, and for whom. This is the number that bounds a live enclave breach: nothing stops an attacker who owns the enclave from asking for one mailbox at a time, so what is available is the rate. Every decision goes through authorize(), which is also the only place a row is written for one, and the count-then-log pair happens under one lock, so two concurrent unwraps cannot both read "59 used" and both proceed. allowed_target() is the other half: a signed DPoP proof is only ever for Google's token endpoint.

The only place the outer wrapping key is derived or a DPoP proof is signed. Both keys arrive through systemd LoadCredentialEncrypted=, sealed to the host TPM and decrypted into $CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY at unit start: no Vault, because a Shamir-sealed Vault starts sealed after every reboot and a fail-closed design plus a human unseal means no mail moves until someone wakes up. The outer key is per user, HKDF(master, salt=uid), so a future per-user revocation and the per-user audit line mean something.

One SQLite row per co-signer request: what was asked, and what was decided. The enclave cannot rewrite it. Attestation says the right code booted; this says what happened afterwards. Neither prevents anything, but together they bound a breach to what the rate limit allowed and leave evidence of exactly which users were touched. Append-only by convention: no UPDATE and no DELETE appears anywhere in the package.

Lives under the unit's StateDirectory=cosigner, owned by the cosigner user rather than letterlock. What buys something against an attacker who already owns the box is a copy off it, which is the operator's job rather than this module's.

A refusal here is either a bug or a breach in progress, and both want a human looking within minutes. This is the only place the cosigner package touches backend/, and the import is inside the function rather than at module scope for two reasons: the service must start on a box where backend/ is not deployed at all, and when the co-signer moves to its own host under its own operator this function is the only thing to rewrite.

nodes.lbl:
hard dependency by design:
co-signer down = no mail
processed, for anyone
nodes.desc: The availability cost the design accepts in exchange for removing a confidentiality risk. A cached local key or a "proceed anyway" fallback would collapse the whole property back to a single box holding everything. Until the enclave moves to Phala this is separation of privilege on one box (a second unix account, its own drop-in, its own credentials), not separation of operator, and no product copy may say otherwise.
The mailbox itself. Read through the history cursor, written as drafts (never sent) and as calendar events with no attendees (so no invites go out).
Delivers {emailAddress, historyId} with an OIDC bearer JWT attached, to the public webhook endpoint on API_HOST. The watch expires after about seven days, which is why the renewal timer exists.

Verifies the Pub/Sub OIDC JWT (issuer, audience, pushing service account, expiry) through Google's tokeninfo endpoint. The endpoint is public, so claims are screened locally first: anything whose payload does not already carry the right issuer, audience, service account and an unexpired exp is rejected without touching Google, which is what stops an anonymous flood from turning into an outbound flood and getting us throttled. Verified tokens are cached until they expire, so Pub/Sub's own retries cost nothing. The historyId in the push is not used: the daemon pulls the delta from the account's stored cursor.

The FIFO wake is a content-free byte: it says work arrived but not for whom. This spool carries the routing key. enqueue is append-only under an exclusive lock; drain reads-then-truncates under the same lock, so a push landing mid-drain is either fully included or left for the next wake, never lost or half-read. Multiple wakes between drains coalesce, deduped by account id.

The always-on drafter, run by email-daemon.service with Restart=always. Blocks on state/wake.fifo. The read end stays open for the whole process lifetime, so a poke arriving mid-processing is never refused. The FIFO is 0600: it was 0666 back when the webhook was PHP running as a different user, and leaving it world-writable now would just let any local account wake the daemon.

Single source of truth for per-account realtime processing, so the fetch, the routing and the cursor advance live in exactly one place no matter which entry point woke the box. Splits the fetched mail into bot requests (forwarded to the account's own plus-alias) and everything else, runs sent mail through scheduling only for accounts that opted in, and advances lastHistoryId at the end. log and notify_err are injected so each entry point keeps its own logging.

Persistent per-account state for the push pipeline: {lastHistoryId, watchExpiration}. Keyed by file path, one store per account, so a shared process holds independent cursors per user. The cursor is also the dedup guarantee the drafting and scheduling paths rely on, since history delivers each message exactly once.

Daemon runtime scratch, grouped under state/ rather than dropped beside the source so a deploy can reason about "code" and "not code" by directory. Created on first write by paths.ensure_run_dir(); never synced or deleted by deploy.sh.

A Gmail push watch expires after about seven days, so every account needs users.watch re-registered on a schedule. renew_account is also called at onboarding for the just-registered account, so registration and renewal share one code path. Run for every active account by gmail-watch.timer.

Every Gmail and Calendar call in the app starts here, and every one of them starts from an Account: there is no ambient mailbox any more. Credentials are constructed with no refresh token at all, which routes every token acquisition through the refresh_handler in backend.custody.tokens. Putting a refresh token in that object would defeat split custody for as long as the object lives.

Two entry points, matching the two modes the system has: fetch_since_history for realtime processing off the cursor (returning received mail, sent mail, the new historyId, and a stale flag when the cursor is too old to resolve), and fetch_daily for the summary's last-24-hours sweep. Both are per account.

The RFC822 assembly (multipart/alternative, a plain part and an HTML part carrying Gmail's own gmail_quote markup and attribution line, so a draft opened in the web UI collapses the quote the way a native reply does) plus drafts.create / drafts.update. The update path is what makes progressive drafts work.
events.list and events.insert. One consent covers Gmail and Calendar, so the service comes from gmail_api rather than being built a second way here.

Triggered by forwarding an email to the account's own plus-alias (user+bot@…) with optional context typed at the top. Splits out the user's context and the original message metadata, finds the original thread by from+subject, and drafts a reply on that thread. The alias is derived per account rather than hardcoded: it used to be the box owner's literal address, checked against every account's mail, so no other user could trigger the path and the owner's alias could fire inside someone else's mailbox.

Classifies which incoming mail warrants a personal reply, then drafts it. Also the home of the shapes every draft caller shares: drafting_instructions() (the voice profile then the owner's personal facts, one assembly so both paths hand the model the same brief), build_draft_payload(), submit_draft(), gmail_thread_link() and format_draft_line().

Calls the model with tool schemas and lets it decide which to invoke, looping until it returns a final draft or MAX_ITERATIONS is hit. untrusted() is the fence put around anything that came from outside the account (email bodies, tool results) before it reaches the model, paired with INJECTION_RULE in the system prompt. dashes_banned(account) is consulted here and is what puts the PUNCTUATION RULE in the prompt, so the model is told the rule exactly when we enforce it by rejecting the draft.

Executors for the tools the drafter can call. Errors come back as error dicts rather than raising, so a failed lookup is something the model can read and recover from instead of losing the whole draft. The account is passed in rather than looked up: the drafter is already holding it, and a tool that could resolve its own account would be a tool that could reach a mailbox nobody asked it to.

Every voice profile question: where a profile lives, which one applies (resolve()), and how one is generated from the account's own sent mail. Samples come from the Sent label, quoted replies and signatures cut, one-liners and forwards dropped, capped per correspondent so one thread cannot define the profile. DEFAULT_CONSTRAINTS is written into the document when it is first created, never appended at prompt time, so a rule the user edits or deletes is a rule the drafter stops following.

The generated or hand-edited profile, beside that user's credentials and state. Never in config/, which deploy.sh overwrites from the operator's ~/.system_files on every push, so a profile written there would disappear on the next deploy. account.set_voice() is the sole writer of the manifest pointer.

The second document: facts the owner writes about themselves, read into every draft prompt beneath the voice profile. A drafter that knows the voice perfectly still cannot answer "which afternoon suits you?". Kept apart from the profile because voice_dna.generate() overwrites that one wholesale and these facts must survive it.

Derived path, no manifest pointer, which is why account._owned_paths() owns the account's whole directory rather than a list of manifest keys: a key list would have left a deleted user's personal information on disk.

Operator prompts pushed from ~/.system_files by deploy.sh: the summary prompt and the operator's own voice profile. paths.config_file() prefers the deployed copy and falls back to ~/.system_files, so the same code path serves the box and a laptop checkout. Reachable only through the operator's own manifest entry; everyone else gets backend/drafting/default_voice.md until they generate or write their own.

Turns sent mail into calendar events, but only for accounts that switched auto_schedule on: writing to someone's calendar without being asked is a surprise. An email becomes an event only when it commits to a concrete date and clock time. Events are created on the primary calendar with no attendees, so no invites are sent. Dedup comes from the history cursor upstream, the same guarantee the drafting path relies on.

Masking runs in one of two modes and new_state() is where that is decided: with the Presidio + spaCy analyzer installed it does NER; without it, or for an account that switched it off, regexes cover secrets, emails and phone numbers. Both modes run the deterministic layers first and both allocate tags through _tag_value(), so a restore works either way. Measured recall on the public corpus is 96% with the analyzer and 74% without, the whole gap being PERSON. The tag mapping is the sensitive artifact: it lives in memory for one draft and is never persisted or sent.

The provider catalog, the model, the thinking mode, the reasoning effort and the masking boundary in one place. make_client(account) is the only constructor and resolve(account) the only chooser; a stated per-account preference is honored or it raises, never substituted, because standing in a different provider would send that user's mail somewhere they did not agree to. Every call is /v1/chat/completions and none is /v1/responses, which is stateful and persists content server-side; a test reads the tree as an AST and fails if anything reaches for it.
Proxy for secrets.load() (see the ✳ node): DEEPSEEK_API_KEY, and NEARAI_API_KEY which serves both NEAR AI providers. A provider whose key is absent is not offered in Settings and cannot be selected.

Fetches the provider's report with a nonce generated seconds ago and requires three bindings: report_data carries the response signing address, report_data carries our nonce, and the enclave's stated model_name matches the model asked for. RTMR3 measures only NEAR's bootstrap compose, not the model server, so ComposeLog closes the gap: the endpoint publishes a second quote over actions_hash, the hash is recomputed from the action log rather than read, and every compose still running must appear in the allowlist pinned by file content. One hostname is a pool, so the verdict cache keys on signing address plus instance id plus actions_hash, otherwise a load balancer would be the bypass.

The committed pin list, so authorizing an image is a reviewed diff. rt_mr3 moves whenever NEAR redeploys the bootstrap and several images sit behind one hostname, so expect more than one pin per model; a drift fails closed. Re-pin with `python -m backend.integrations.inference_attestation <provider>`, read the diff, commit. Still unclosed above this: a compose names container images by digest, and digest → reviewed source needs the build's Sigstore/SLSA provenance.
Proxy for backend/tee/quote_policy.py (see the ✳ node): the same five checks, pointed outward at the provider about to read a user's mail.
The default provider, called directly. Nothing about it is verifiable, which is exactly why the masking layer applies on every provider rather than only on this one.

nodes.lbl:
NEAR AI per-model endpoints
glm-5-2 / gpt-oss-120b
nodes.desc: Per-model direct completions endpoints, each a dstack CVM that publishes a TDX quote. The cloud-api.near.ai gateway is deliberately not used: a per-model endpoint is the only shape whose attestation can say which model it serves, and the gateway's attestation endpoint is authenticated and answers for the fleet.

Sweeps every active account, fetching each user's mailbox through mailbox.fetch_daily and delivering to account.telegram. It used to be single-tenant in a way that could not be noticed from outside: the fetch inherited the process environment and the send carried no target, so every account past the first got no summary and the operator got theirs. Both boundaries are now per account.

send_telegram(msg, target) always takes an explicit target; there is deliberately no environment fallback on the per-account path, because a fallback there delivers one user's mail metadata to whoever the box owner is. operator_target() is the separate, deliberate exception for box-level failures. Linking a chat is a verification rather than a text field: the UI shows a one-time code, the user sends it to the bot, and the chat id stored is one we have seen them post from.
Proxy for secrets.load() (see the ✳ node): TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN, plus the operator's own chat id for box-level failures.
Where notifications land: what was drafted, what was scheduled, the daily summary, and box-level failures to the operator's own chat.
